### THE
# PUBLISHER
### TO THE
# READER.

THOUGH it may well seem needless to provide a particular preface for these *Three First Dialogues*, as we have been largely preceded by what is already noted in general in the *Palæopolite’s* <note>original: "Palæopolite"; likely referring to the author's pseudonym, meaning "citizen of the ancient city."</note> Epistle to his Friend; yet because the other two dialogues did not leave my hands without a somewhat larger preamble, I have thought it appropriate to preface these with a brief commendation. 

Briefly then, the subject of the first of these three dialogues is the *Attributes of God*; the subject of the latter two is the *Adjusting of the Phenomena of the World to the Goodness of his Providence*. These are arguments that will easily attract the attention of the curious, and I believe they are handled with such clarity, such full comprehension, and such careful circumspection that they will also satisfy the ingenious <note>original: "Ingenuous"; in this context, it refers to people who are honorable, open-minded, or intellectually well-bred.</note>. 

However, those who are determined to find flaws will easily imagine they see them even where they do not exist. The main goal of the author in handling the *Attributes of God* seems to be to navigate with such caution and judgment as to avoid lessening the *Majesty of the Godhead* by a pretense of making his *Nature* so universally intelligible <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "telligible."</note>—

<summary>The publisher introduces the first three dialogues of the collection, which focus on the attributes of God and the reconciliation of worldly phenomena with divine providence.</summary>
<keywords>Attributes of God, Divine Providence, Palæopolite, Preface, Theology, Philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the publisher’s preface, completing the sentence from the previous page regarding the balance between making God's nature understandable and maintaining His majesty.</meta>

->### The Publisher to the Reader.<-

<margin>John 4:22</margin>
intelligible to all capacities whatsoever (for it is well known how dull and short-sighted some people are), nor yet, on the other side, to make his existence incredible by puzzling and confounding even the best understandings with high-flown notions and harsh contradictions—even perfect inconsistencies—under the pretense of magnifying the *Nature of God* even more. It is as if the more perplexed and self-contradictory the *Nature of God* were, the more glorious and adorable he would be. If that were true, our Savior’s words to the *Samaritans* would not have been a rebuke, but a compliment <note>original: "Encomium"</note>, when he says, *You worship what you do not know*. Yet this is exactly the condition of all those who dress up the Deity with conflicting attributes; it is an invitation to those prone to atheism <note>original: "Atheistically given"</note> to abandon both the Deity and his worship at once.

I believe this consideration led the author of these dialogues not only to use sound reason to defeat, but also to explode with a fitting and proper contempt, that newly-invented opinion of the *Nullubists* <note>original: "Nullubists"; from the Latin 'nullibi' (nowhere). This refers to philosophers, like René Descartes and his followers, who argued that God and the soul are incorporeal and therefore exist nowhere in space.</note>. These people imagine themselves to be so much more *intellectual* than others by declaring that *God is nowhere*, even though they cannot deny that he exists. In this lofty adventure, though they boast that they are safely elevated above the region of *imagination*, I have no doubt that this high flight of their thoughts will eventually be found to be nothing more than a swollen bubble on troubled waters. The *levity* and *puffiness* of their spirits have carried their concepts (if they have any concept at all of what they are talking about) far above the level of common sense and reason.

In his *adjusting* of the *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of the *universe* to *Divine Goodness*, it is notable that he has avoided no difficulties that human wit can imagine or invent. Instead, he has brought them all into view—or at least the hardest of them all—and provided such examples <note>original: "Specimina"</note> of every kind that, in all likelihood,

# The Publisher to the Reader.

Whatever new instances may occur to men, or whatever they may intentionally devise <note>original: "excogitate"</note>, will be easily satisfied by the solution of these preceding examples.

It should also not be overlooked <note>original: "pretermitted"</note> how he has fitted *solutions* and *hypotheses* to the various degrees and capacities of the minds of men, so that the argument may not be too large for some, nor too small for others. I will say nothing of how, in representing the gross barbarities of the manners and religions in the uncivilized parts of the world, he uses a not unpleasant *satirical tone* to dexterously endeavor to awaken the civilized parts of the world into a sense of abhorrence for even the least shadow or resemblance of those cursed <note>original: "execrable"</note> barbarities.

And this again, I think, is very sober and humane: in setting out these *geniuses* <note>term: "Genius" here refers to a person's natural disposition or character type</note> of several sorts and sizes, as I just mentioned, there is no reproach cast upon any. He who does not have the fate to be a *Philotheus* <note>note: Greek for "Lover of God"</note> or a *Bathynous* <note>note: Greek for "Deep-minded"</note> is nonetheless allowed to be a *Sophron* <note>note: Greek for "Discreet" or "Self-controlled"</note>. All of these dispositions in their own way are laudable and honorable; it is certainly a lack of judgment or good nature that makes them despise one another. 

For those who have arrived at any true measure of real piety and virtue find such great perfection in that state, that when they see others who have reached the same degree as themselves, they will easily give them the right hand of fellowship and acknowledge them as equals, regardless of what their other intellectual capacities may be. 

But for those whose either *knowledge* or *ignorance* is accompanied by such a high degree of rudeness and immorality that they despise and reproach all who are not of their own size in *either* category, it is only just if they find themselves lightly criticized <note>original: "perstringed"</note> in the parable of those two loud-singing nightingales of *Arcadia* <note>note: A reference to a pastoral region in Greece, often used to symbolize a rustic or poetic setting</note> that so rudely awakened *Bathynous* out of his divine dream.

<summary>The publisher explains that the author tailors his arguments to different intellectual capacities and uses satire to discourage barbarism, while emphasizing that moral virtue is more important than intellectual status.</summary>
<keywords>Philotheus, Bathynous, Sophron, Arcadia, religious tolerance, virtue vs. intellect, satire, character types</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the publisher’s preface, detailing the character development and the use of physiognomy in the dialogues, while touching upon the author's critique of René Descartes.</meta>

# The Publisher to the Reader.

Lastly, regarding the observation of *decorum* <note>term: "Decorum" refers to the literary principle of making a character's speech and behavior fit their social status and personality</note> among the characters: although it is not neglected or violated in any part of all the five dialogues, it is more complete and articulate in these first three. The specific character of *Hylobares* <note>note: Greek for "heavy with matter," representing a materialist character</note> had no opportunity to clearly show himself in the last two. However, the characters of all the others are more or less discernible in all five, but most of all that of *Cuphophron* <note>note: Greek for "light-minded," representing a more airy or superficial thinker</note>. 

In the character of this person, the *author* <note>original: "Dramatist"</note> seems to have been wise even to the point of *physiognomic* curiosity, suggesting that he is a man of very small stature. This fits excellently well with that cheerful manner, that quick wit, and that lighthearted humor that reveals itself from the beginning to the end in the person of *Cuphophron*. According to the rules of *physiognomy* <note>term: "Physiognomy" was the historical practice of judging a person's character or temperament from their physical features</note>, this disposition is most common in men of small stature, as their internal heat and spirits are somewhat large in proportion to the size of their bodies. This makes them quick and cheerful, and of sudden understanding, though prone to <note>original: "obnoxious to"</note> fits of intense emotion <note>original: "Raptures"</note> and lofty daydreams <note>original: "exalted Resveries"</note>, even if they often fall short or overshoot the mark and do not easily find the truth. 

This, therefore, agrees well with the *Platonic* nature of *Cuphophron's* intellect. Additionally, it may be that the author had some regard for the small stature of René Descartes <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note>, of whose wisdom *Cuphophron* is presented as such an excessive admirer—as if smaller bodies were the most suitable case for a *Cartesian* wit. Furthermore, one should note that *Plato* was also not of tall <note>original: "procere"</note> stature.

Several such clever details <note>original: "Prettinesses"</note> accompany the thorough pursuit of the main subject of these dialogues. In this, I think the author will not easily seem to have overreached in the eyes of open-minded and honest readers, except perhaps in his very direct and open opposition to that much-admired philosopher René Descartes <note>original: "Renatus Des-Cartes"</note>, on whom per—

<summary>The publisher explains the use of "decorum" in character building, specifically how the character Cuphophron's small stature and lively temperament reflect the principles of physiognomy and mirror the traits of philosophers like Descartes and Plato.</summary>
<keywords>Decorum, Hylobares, Cuphophron, Physiognomy, René Descartes, Plato, characterization, Cartesianism</keywords>

# The Publisher to the Reader.

<sig>A 4</sig>

...sons well versed in philosophical speculations have bestowed such high praises <note>original: "Encomiums"</note>, especially a writer of our own. This writer, besides the many commendations he adorns him with throughout his writings, compares him (in his *Appendix* to the defense of his *Philosophical Cabbala*) to *Bezaleel* and *Aholiab* <note>Biblical craftsmen from the Book of Exodus, inspired by God to build the Tabernacle</note>, as if he were inspired from above with a wit so curiously mechanical as to frame such a consistent structure of *mechanical philosophy* as he did. 

Furthermore, the late learned author of *Philosophy the Interpreter of Scripture* <note>original: "Philosophia Scripturæ Interpres"</note>, after a laborious, subtle, and extensive effort to prove that philosophy is the best interpreter of the Bible—as if all that effort had been intended on behalf of *Descartes* <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note> to place him in the infallible chair of authority—concludes at last with a very high and unparalleled eulogy of the *Cartesian philosophy*. Therefore, it may very well be questioned whether it was wise for the writer of these *Dialogues* to risk his own reputation by so openly opposing and attacking the great name and authority of such a famous and eminent philosopher as *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>.

But for my part, I must confess that the more he may have exposed himself by this freedom (provided that he is in the right, which the impartial reader must judge), the points that are debated are of such great consequence that I think his actions are a more conspicuous act of virtue. I believe that the very reasoning used to accuse him of over-reaching is a principle to be abhorred by all good and generous spirits; namely, the idea that it is imprudent to care less for one's own private reputation than for the glory of God and the public good, or the idea that anyone should lose respect for doing what is truly worthy and praiseworthy.

<summary>The publisher acknowledges the immense popularity and perceived divine inspiration of Descartes' mechanical philosophy but defends the author of the current work for having the courage to challenge such a famous figure for the sake of truth and the public good.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Cartesian philosophy, mechanical philosophy, Bezaleel and Aholiab, Philosophical Cabbala, intellectual courage, reputation vs. truth</keywords>

# The Publisher to the Reader.

Besides, he only follows the pattern of that very author who is observed to have so highly commended *Descartes*; most of the allegations against his philosophy are more fully pursued in that *eulogist's* <note>original: "Encomiast's"</note> writings. And in that very epistle to *V. C.* <note>likely Victor Clerselier, a French editor and defender of Descartes</note> where he makes it his business to apologize for him, and to extol him and magnify him to the skies, yet he does plainly and openly declare, *That it is a kind of vile and abject worship of matter* <note>original: "$\upsilon\lambda o\lambda\alpha\tau\rho\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha$" (hylolatria)</note>, *or superstitious idolizing of matter, to pretend that all the phenomena of the universe will arise out of it by mere mechanical motion*. And yet in the same epistle, he seems to acknowledge that there may be some few effects that are purely mechanical. I believe this came from his over-great desire to make *Descartes* seem as significant as he could with any judgment and conscience. But for my part, after more seriously considering what occurs in these dialogues, I am abundantly assured that there is no purely mechanical *phenomenon* in the whole universe.

<margin>Exodus 35:35</margin>
Nor should that author be understood as comparing *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note> with *Bezalel* and *Oholiab* <note>Biblical craftsmen chosen by God to build the Tabernacle</note> as if he really believed he was supernaturally inspired. For how could anyone apply that sense to such a high-flown compliment, when he plainly and zealously refutes *Descartes* throughout his works wherever he finds him faulty in matters of concern, just as he praises and commends him where he deserves it? This is a clear indication he did not take him to be infallibly inspired. And it may be that the correct *interpretation* <note>original: "Exegesis"</note> of *Bezalel* and *Oholiab* being filled with the *Spirit of God* is simply their being filled with *wisdom of heart* for those mechanical curiosities of work; as it is signified toward the end of that chapter, that they had a special and extraordinary *natural talent* <note>original: "Genius"</note> that way, which was the gift

<summary>The publisher argues that while the author previously praised Descartes, he always rejected the idea that the universe is purely mechanical, and his comparisons of Descartes to Biblical figures were compliments of talent rather than claims of divine inspiration.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, mechanical philosophy, hylolatria, Bezalel and Oholiab, divine inspiration, natural genius, physics vs. spirituality</keywords>

# The Publisher to the Reader.

<margin>Exodus 35:31</margin>
<margin>*Antidote*, Book 2, Chapter 2, Sections 7–14; Chapter 12, Sections 1–3, etc. *Immortality of the Soul*, Book 3, Chapters 12 and 13.</margin>
...indication that he looked upon it as a gift of God in Nature. Besides, every great thing in Nature, according to the *Hebrew* idiom, takes its name from God. Therefore, to be filled with the *Spirit of God in wisdom and understanding, etc.* is to possess a great measure of *wisdom* and *understanding* in those specific things. Just as, without question, *Descartes* <note>original: "Des-Cartes"</note> possessed a great deal of *intelligence* and *insight* <note>original: "Wit and Sagacity"</note> to discover the most plausible *material causes* for the *phenomena* <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of the world, and to organize them into the most impressive framework <note>original: "specious Contexture"</note> possible to create a mechanical philosophy. But this great *admirer* <note>original: "Encomiast"</note> of his declares as plainly in several places—just as the author <note>original: "Contriver"</note> of these current dialogues does—that these things can neither arise nor hold together without a higher principle to superintend and guide them.

But regarding the author of *Philosophy, the Interpreter of Scripture* <note>original: "Philosophia Scripturæ Interpres"; a controversial 1666 work often attributed to Lodewijk Meyer which argued that philosophy should be the tool for biblical interpretation</note>, I must confess I am quite surprised <note>original: "much admire"</note> that, after working so hard to prove his argument, he should choose *Descartes’* philosophy as such a reliable oracle for interpreting the meaning of Scripture. It is true that several aspects of it are very fittingly applied to a philosophical interpretation of the six-day Creation. However, those are elements already included in the *Pythagorean* framework of the universe and they correspond with the ancient *Cabbala* <note>The "Cabbala" here refers to the idea of a secret, mystical tradition of divine knowledge supposedly passed down from Moses</note>; they are not new inventions of *Cartesian* intelligence. The truth is, what makes *Descartes’* philosophy look so impressive <note>original: "augustly"</note> is that he has interwoven into it that noble system of the world according to the tradition of *Pythagoras* and his followers—or, if you prefer, the most ancient *Cabbala* of *Moses*. But the rest of his philosophy is more *clever* <note>original: "pretty"</note> than *great*; and in the sense that he intends—that of pure mechanism—it is enormously and ridiculously false.

<summary>The publisher argues that Descartes' brilliance was a natural gift but notes that his mechanical philosophy only succeeds where it aligns with ancient Pythagorean and Mosaic traditions. He critiques those who use Cartesianism as the primary lens for interpreting the Bible, calling pure mechanism "ridiculously false."</summary>

<keywords>René Descartes, Mechanical Philosophy, Biblical Interpretation, Pythagoras, Cabbala, Moses, Material Causes, Phenomena</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the publisher's critique of René Descartes' philosophical principles, specifically focusing on how his theories of matter and motion conflict with traditional Christian theology and scripture.</meta>

# The Publisher to the Reader.

But now, regarding those principles or passages in his philosophy that are more uniquely his own, there is nothing more alienated from the spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the Scripture and the service of theology than they are. For fuller satisfaction, and for the sake of the pleasantness <note>original: "suavity"</note> of the concepts, let us test a few. 

It is a grand principle with him that wherever we cannot help but conceive of an extension or expansion, we must likewise necessarily conceive that there is matter. Therefore, because we cannot help but conceive of an indefinite space extended all around us, we cannot help but conceive of matter extended everywhere. This plainly implies that we cannot help but conceive that matter exists, regardless of what else exists. From this it follows that the existence of matter is necessary in itself and independent of God, because in its very notion or idea, it cannot be conceived of as non-existent; we are unable to imagine anything other than an indefinite extension all around us. How this will agree with the absolute perfection of God, or what kind of sound meaning it will provide for the first verse of *Genesis* <note>"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."</note>, I leave to anyone to guess.

Again, it is an equally admitted principle with him that matter alone—with the degree of motion that is supposed to exist now in the universe—will produce all the phenomena <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of the world: the sun, moon, and stars, air, water, earth, plants, animals, and the bodies of men, in the exact order and organization in which they are found. ### *Of Father Euistor, the Palæopolite <term>Palæopolite: A name derived from Greek meaning "citizen of an ancient city."</term>, to a Noble Friend of his regarding the following Dialogues.*

*Reader,*

I believe you will wonder at the backwards <note>original: "preposterous"</note> order of my publishing these **two** *dialogues* before the first three have seen the light of day. # The Publisher to the Reader.

Holy days in the Christian calendar <note>original: "Kalendar"</note> are consistent enough with these *Divine Dialogues* in both purpose and title. In these dialogues, the writer has always followed this method: to add a practical application for the improvement of life to every *historical narrative*. Whether in verse or prose, if this method were diligently followed when handling the historical articles of our Christian faith, it would be so powerful in making people good that I do not doubt that *Philotheus* <note>The pseudonym for the author, Henry More (1614–1687), a Cambridge Platonist</note>—had he thought of it—would have added this as a ninth instruction aimed at hastening those happy times for the Church which he predicts.

Reader, if you are willing to accept these works kindly for now, it will further encourage the author to allow what still remains in his possession to be published <note>original: "see the Light"</note> in due time. He will then be as willing to satisfy the *philosophical spirit* <note>original: "Philosophical Genius"</note> in those first three dialogues as he has been eager to edify the religious spirit in these.

->G. C.<- <note>These initials likely belong to the publisher or an editor associated with Henry More's circle.</note>

# The proper Characters of the Persons in the ensuing <note>original: "ensuiug"</note> Dialogues, with some Allusion to their Names.

---

**Philotheus**: A zealous and sincere lover of God and **Christ**, and of the whole creation. <note>The name comes from the Greek *Philo* (lover) and *Theos* (God).</note>

*Bathynous*: The deeply thoughtful or profoundly thinking man. <note>From the Greek *Bathys* (deep) and *Nous* (mind).</note>

*Sophron*: The sober and cautious <note>original: "wary"</note> man. <note>From the Greek *Sophron*, meaning of sound mind or temperate.</note>

*Philopolis*: The pious and loyal politician. <note>From the Greek *Philo* (lover) and *Polis* (city or state).</note>

*Euistor*: A man of criticism, philology <note>The study of language and literature</note>, and history. <note>From the Greek *Eu* (well) and *Histor* (learned or knowing).</note>

*Hylobares*: A young, witty, and morally upright <note>original: "well-moralized"</note> materialist. <note>From the Greek *Hyle* (matter) and *Baros* (heavy), suggesting someone "weighed down by matter."</note>

*Cuphophron*: A zealous but airy-minded *Platonist* and *Cartesian* <note>A follower of the philosophy of René Descartes</note>, or *mechanist*. <note>From the Greek *Kouphos* (light or nimble) and *Phron* (mind).</note>

*Ocymo*: *Cuphophron*’s servant boy, so called because of his nimbleness. <note>From the Greek *Okymos*, meaning swift.</note>

## The general Character.

All are free spirits, mutually permitting one another the liberty of philosophizing without any breach of friendship.

Hylobares interposes his queries: first, concerning the existence of God and divine providence.

*Hyl.* This would be an excellent temperament in *Philopolis* indeed—to be so resolved—if he were sure not to fall short in his account.

*Philop:* For my part, gentlemen, I could never yet bring myself to doubt such truths, though *Hylobares* has several times attempted to unsettle <note>original: "dissettle"</note> me at my house near the "other Athens" <note>A common 17th-century reference to a university town like Oxford or Cambridge</note>, where he sometimes honors me with a visit. # DIVINE DIALOGUES.

### Page 18

*Philotheus.* Therefore, wherever we find frequent and repeated indications of skillfully pursuing a design, we must acknowledge that some intelligent being is the cause of it.

*Hylobares.* We must indeed.

*Philotheus.* But what a small scroll and how few instances of pursuing a design are there in that treatise by Archimedes <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was a Greek mathematician; the treatise mentioned is likely *On the Sphere and Cylinder*</note>, in comparison to the entire volume of Nature? In Archimedes' work, every proof leading to the final result (which is the proportion between the sphere and the cylinder) is a testament to the wit and reason of that mathematician. In the same way, the various subordinate parts of nature in the world—which are practically infinite—conspicuously carry within them a design for the best. Therefore, they are a "cloud of witnesses" <note>A biblical reference to Hebrews 12:1, meaning a large group of spectators or evidence</note> that there is a divine and intellectual principle underlying everything.

*Hylobares.* This is better understood through examples, *Philotheus*.

<margin>VI. Several examples of that general argument.</margin>
*Philotheus.* It is. And I will provide examples of the simplest ones first—I mean the most broad and general strokes of the skill of that "Great Geometrician," as Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46–119 CE) was a Greek philosopher; he famously wrote that "God always geometrizes"</note> somewhere calls the Deity. 

1. For example, consider the nature of **gravity**, which pulls dense terrestrial matter downward through both air and water. Without this power, no beasts or birds could live upon the earth or in the air, because dirt and filth would float into their mouths and stop their breathing; nor could fish exist in the water. 

2. Consider also the strong resistance against the presence of too much "subtle matter" <note>original: "subtilest Matter." In 17th-century physics, this referred to a very thin, weightless substance (aether) thought to fill space</note> in these lower regions. This thinner element is ill-suited for the lungs of either birds or beasts, as is more fully understood through those excellent experiments with the air-pump <note>A reference to Robert Boyle’s 1650s experiments proving that air is necessary for life and combustion</note>. 

3. Finally, consider the parallelism and the properly proportioned tilt of the Earth's axis, and the latitude of the Moon from the equator.

*Hylobares.* I cannot deny that these laws are better than if things had been otherwise.

*Bath.* And I believe this necessary existence of God is the most solid understanding of His eternal duration. This duration cannot strictly or formally be called "successive," but only "virtually" and "applicatively." The riverbed itself does not flow away in a sequence, even though the water does. This is the nature of the steady and permanent duration of God’s necessary existence in relation to all successive periods of duration whatsoever.

*Philoth.* I still do not fully understand you, *Bathynous*.

*Bath.* I am saying that "successive duration," properly defined, is incompatible with God, because He is a being who exists by necessity and is therefore without beginning. For whatever is past was once present; and therefore, since every part of this infinite sequence was once present, even the most infinitely distant moment of it was present at some time. *Philoth.* You say truly, *Bathynous*. There must be a *most-remote moment* in any succession, even a *most-infinitely-remote* one in an infinite succession. But since the *most-infinitely-remote* moment cannot be a *connecting limit* <note>original: *Terminus copulans*—a point that joins what came before with what comes after</note>, because there is nothing before it to join with future succession, it must therefore be an *ending limit* <note>original: *Terminus terminans*</note>. And because it must of necessity have once been "now" (present), it is plain that at that present moment was the boundary or beginning of this supposed infinite succession.

Or to put it briefly, to prevent all possible objections against the idea of a *most-infinitely remote* moment in an *infinite* succession—as if such concepts were <term>inconsistent</term> <note>original: *ἀσύστατα* (asystata)</note>—I would rather argue in this way: namely, that because all the moments past in an infinite succession were at some point present, it follows plainly that all the moments in this infinite succession (or at least all but one) were at some point still to come. And if either all these moments, or all but one, were once "to come," it is manifest that the whole sequence—or at least the whole sequence except for one single moment—was once in the future, and therefore had a beginning. 

I understand the strength of your reasoning very well. And therefore, when I spoke of the successive duration of *God*, I did not mean "succession" in that *proper* and *formal* sense (as if God moves from one moment to the next), but only a "virtual," "applicative," or "relative" succession, as you might have gathered from some of my expressions. The duration of *God* is like that of a *rock*, but the duration of *natural* things is like that of a *river*; their succession passes <term>like a river</term> <note>original: *ποταμοῦ δίκην* (potamou diken)</note>, as the philosopher *Heraclitus* says. Therefore, those who attribute *successive* duration (properly so called) to the steady permanency of a necessary Self-existence seem like those who imagine the shore is moving because their ship is in motion.

<header>DIVINE DIALOGUES.</header>

We project our own fluid, successive sense of duration onto the steady permanency of the eternal duration of God. His duration—though steady, permanent, and without any flowing away or sequence of moments (being, in fact, nothing other than His necessary self-existence)—is nevertheless such that even the most infinite span of past time can never reach beyond it, nor can any future time ever exhaust it. From this, it is plain that although the eternal duration of God is truly permanent, it cannot be a single, indivisible instant that is perfectly identical to itself in every regard, failing to encompass all possible successive developments that occur in time.

# DIVINE DIALOGUES.

I have only one more doubt <note>original: "Scruple"</note> concerning God's eternity, and then I will move on to the next attribute. The eternal succession of God's existence seems to imply a contradiction. For unless every specified part is infinite, the whole cannot be infinite. And if every specified part—suppose the tenth, the hundredth, or the thousandth—is infinite, then there would be many infinites.

*Philotheus:* I understand you very well. But you must consider that either God has existed from eternity <note>original: "ab aeterno"</note>, or the world has. Since it is certain that something must be eternal, it is no contradiction that God should be so. So you see, there is no more confusion or difficulty regarding God’s existence than there would be if He were not in the world—following the last of my preliminary guidelines <note>original: "Advertisements"</note>. Indeed, the most unsolvable puzzle of all would be to accept a world existing from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note> without God. For an eternal flow of movement in matter would be "eternal succession" in the strict sense, which *Bathynous* cleverly suggested is impossible. And if matter ever stood still and was later moved, there must be a First Mover distinct from the matter. This seems to logically imply there is a God; even more so because if matter existed on its own, it must have been eternally at rest before it began to move.

*Hylobares:* This difficulty has vanished so suddenly that I am halfway ashamed I ever proposed it.

*Philotheus:* I have met many people to whom this would have seemed like a significant difficulty, so it was not unworthy of being brought up.

*Philopolis:* But I ask you to proceed to the next attribute, *Hylobares*, for I am greatly pleased to see *Philotheus*'s success.

<margin>XXIX. *The essential properties of matter.*</margin>

*Hylobares:* I understand the concept <note>original: "Notion"</note> well enough. But what makes you attribute *disunity* to matter rather than a firm union of parts, especially since you attribute *self-inactivity* to it?

*Philotheus:* Because there is no bond <note>original: *Vinculum*</note> imaginable in matter to hold the parts together. For you know they are impenetrable, and therefore touch one another only at their smooth surfaces <note>original: *Superficies*</note>. How, therefore, can they hold together? What is the principle of their *union*?

*Cuphophron:* Oh, that is very clear, *Philotheus*; that stupendous genius <note>original: "Wit"</note> *Descartes* plainly tells us that it is *rest*.

*Philotheus:* But please tell me, *Cuphophron*, what is *rest*?

*Cuphophron:* That is easily understood from *motion*, which *Descartes* suggests <note>original: "intimates"</note> to be the separation or movement <note>original: "translation"</note> of one part of matter from another.

*Philotheus:* And so *rest* is the *union* or *unseparateness* of one part of matter from another.

*Cuphophron:* I can imagine nothing else by it. For if a whole mass of matter moves together as one hard piece, the whole is moved; but the parts in relation to one another, because they do not separate from one another, are said to rest. And on this account *motion* is said to be reciprocal, because indeed separation is so.

*Philotheus:* Then *rest* and the *unseparateness* of parts are one and the same.

*Cuphophron:* It seems so.

*Philotheus:* And *unseparateness* and *union* are one and the same.

*Cuphophron:* The very same, I think.

*Philotheus:* Why then *rest* and *union* are one and the same, and so the principle of the *union* of the parts of matter is the *union* of their parts.

*Hylobares:* That is, they have no principle of *union* at all, and therefore by themselves are disunited.

*Philotheus:* And there is great reason they should have none, forasmuch as they are to be bound together—

<summary>Philotheus critiques the Cartesian view that "rest" is the force that holds matter together, arguing that this definition is circular and fails to provide a real mechanism for the cohesion of physical parts. He suggests that matter is inherently disunited and lacks an internal principle of union.</summary>

<margin>30. The true notion of a spirit.</margin>

*Philotheus:* Can you then fail to grasp the true notion of a *spirit*?

*Philotheus:* Excellently defined.

This is evident in the nature of God, whose very concept <note>original: *Idea*</note> implies inseparability, since the opposite would be such an obvious imperfection. For whatever can be torn apart is also capable of being moved. *Philotheus:* I believe we all agree, *Cuphophron*. But I must continue my discussion with *Hylobares*: What do you understand by *self-activity* in a *spirit*, *Hylobares*?

*Hylobares:* I understand it to be an active power in a *spirit*, by which it either changes itself according to its own nature, or moves *matter* in an orderly way according to certain influences <note>original: "modifications"</note> it impresses upon it. It unites *physical monads* <term>physical monads: a term used in 17th-century philosophy to describe the smallest, indivisible building blocks of the physical world</term> into particles of a specific size and shape, and guides them in movements that fulfill the purpose of the *spiritual agent*—whether that purpose is consciously thought of or built into its nature. From this, as was said before, we see the reason why both *disunity* and *inactivity* belong to *matter*.

*Philotheus:* A very accurate and concise answered, *Hylobares*. You are so quick at it that you must have certainly thought of these *notions* before now.

*Hylobares:* I have read something of them. But your skillful definition of the *attributes* of *matter* has made me more confident in defining the attributes of a *spirit*—especially now that I can fully accept the belief in its *existence*, which I could never truly do before. And as for the last attribute, which seemed the most puzzling to me—namely, *self-penetrability*—it is now as easy a concept as any. I understand it to mean simply that different *spirits* may occupy the same space, or that a single spirit can shrink its *extension* into a smaller area, so that one part of its essence occupies the same space as another. Through this power, it is able to expand <note>original: "dilate"</note> or contract itself. I can easily see how this could be a property of any created and finite *spirit*, because the *extension* of a spirit is not physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>.

<summary>Hylobares defines "self-activity" and "self-penetrability" as the core attributes of a spirit, explaining how spirits can move matter and occupy or contract within space. This marks a turning point where Hylobares fully accepts the existence of incorporeal substances.</summary>

*Philotheus:* Very true. But did you not observe, *Hylobares*, how I removed *Sympathy* from the capacity of *matter*?

*Hylobares:* I did, *Philotheus*; and from that, I cannot help but conclude that it is located in the *spiritual* or *incorporeal nature*. By this *Sympathy*, I do not mean a mere *compassivity* <note>original: "Compassivity"; the state of being acted upon or feeling together</note>, but rather a *coactivity* <note>original: "Coactivity"; the state of acting together or simultaneous action</note> of the spirit in which it resides. I believe this is of great use in all *perceptive spirits*. Because of this attribute, no matter how or in what circumstances they are affected in one part, they are affected in the same way in every part. Thus, if there were a perceptive spirit of infinite size <note>original: "Amplitude"</note> and an infinitely high level of *sympathy*, whenever any perceptive energy <note>original: "Energy"; an active power or force</note> appeared in this infinite spirit, it would be immediately and necessarily present throughout all of it at once. 

I must confess, *Philotheus*, I have often thought of these ideas <note>original: "Notions"</note> before now, but I could never attribute them to a *spirit*. This was because I could not believe there was any such thing as a *spirit*, since all *extension* <term>extension: the quality of taking up space; materialists argued that only physical matter could be extended</term> seemed to me to be physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note>. But your *Equinoctial Arrow* <note>Equinoctial Arrow: a thought experiment used by Henry More to argue that space is a real, immobile, and incorporeal entity distinct from the matter moving through it</note> has completely struck that error out of my mind. 

The more I think of it, the more unavoidable it seems to me that the extension in the *equinoctial circle*—in which the arrow is carried in a curved <note>original: "curvilinear"</note> motion—is not only an extension distinct from that of the *aerial circle*, but it is an extension of something real and independent of our imagination. Because the arrow is truly carried in such a curved line, and since *we are unable to imagine it otherwise*, we have as much certainty about this as we have about anything. For it is as certainly true as our mental faculties are true: *and we have no greater certainty than that of our faculties*. Thus, the only obstacle that kept me from admitting the existence of spirits was demolished at once by the skillful arguments <note>original: "assaults"</note> of *Philotheus*.

<header>DIVINE DIALOGUES.</header>

<margin>35. The grounds of Cuphophron's paradox (that spirits are nowhere) presented and examined.</margin>

*Hylobares:* Please tell me then, Cuphophron, what mainly moved you to hold the opinion that you do—that no spirit can be anywhere, or that the human soul is *nowhere*?

*Cuphophron:* Oh Hylobares, there are convincing reasons for this apparent paradox, if they meet with a mind capable of understanding them. But the main reasons are these two. First, because the human mind thinks of things that are nowhere—such as various moral, logical, and mathematical truths. Since these truths are of a nature that exists nowhere, the mind that conceives them must necessarily be nowhere as well. The second reason is that *thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>, as thought, is by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> exempt or separated from all physical extension <note>meaning: the quality of taking up space</note>. For even if we doubt whether there is any matter or any extended thing in the world, we are still certain that we are *thinking beings* <note>original: "Recogitantes"</note>. This shows that thought has nothing at all to do with physical extension, nor can it be applied to it; for we perceive ourselves thinking even when we have not the least thought of anything extended in space. Therefore, since our thoughts have no relation or applicability to extension, they have no relation to place; and consequently, neither our thoughts nor our minds are anywhere.

*Hylobares:* I partly understand what you are getting at, Cuphophron, but not well enough to see any strength at all in your reasoning. You can see the weakness of your first argument from this: it would follow just as easily that the human soul or mind is *somewhere* because it thinks of things that are somewhere, as it would that the soul is nowhere because it thinks of things that are nowhere. Besides, those things which you say are nowhere are actually somewhere—I mean those moral, logical, and mathematical truths. For they exist within the mind or soul; and I believe I have already demonstrated to any unbiased listener that the soul is in the body, and the body you—

<summary>Cuphophron argues that the soul exists "nowhere" because it contemplates abstract concepts and because the act of thinking is independent of physical space; Hylobares begins his rebuttal by arguing that the mind's location is tied to the body.</summary>
<keywords>Cuphophron, Hylobares, soul, spirit, cogitation, extension, mathematical truths, dualism, spatiality, philosophy of mind</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the debate between Hylobares and Cuphophron regarding whether the soul occupies a location. Hylobares is currently refuting Cuphophron's claim that spirits are "nowhere" because they are not physical.</meta>

### DIVINE DIALOGUES.

...cannot deny but that it must be somewhere. It is true that some of those Truths, perhaps as they are *Representations*, do not involve Time or Place; but as they are *Operations* <term>the active processes of the mind</term> or *Modes* <term>the specific states or ways a thing exists</term> of a *Subject* or *Substance* <term>the underlying "thing" or entity that possesses qualities</term>, they must be understood to exist within that Substance. And because there is no Substance that lacks at least an *essential Amplitude* <note>original: "essential Amplitude"; meaning the fundamental property of occupying some kind of space or having "spread"</note>, they exist in a Substance that is, in some way, extended. Thus, by virtue of the nature of their Subject, they must necessarily be understood to be somewhere. For the "Mode" of a thing is inseparable from the Thing itself.

**Cuphophron:** But here you are getting ahead of yourself, *Hylobares*, by assuming something I will not grant you—namely, that there is a Substance of the Mind or Soul that is distinct from *Thought* <note>original: "Cogitation"</note>. I say that *Thought* itself is the very Substance of the Soul; therefore, the Soul is just as much "nowhere" as if it had no substance at all.

**Hylobares:** But notice, *Cuphophron*, that by saying *Thought* itself is the very *Substance* of the Soul, you are affirming that the Soul is, in fact, a Substance. And so my argument applies to you once again—even though saying that an *Operation* <note>the act of thinking or doing</note> is the same as a *Substance* is clearly false. For the Operations of the Soul are distinctly different from one another; if such distinct Operations followed one another, then according to your logic, they would be a series of different Substances following one another. In that case, your Soul would not always be the same *specific substance*, let alone the same *individual* soul. Nothing could be more wild or absurd than that. Furthermore, everyone considers the Soul to be a *permanent thing*, but its Operations are in a state of *flux* and *succession* <note>meaning they are constantly changing and following one after another</note>. How then can these changing thoughts be the Soul itself? If they were, what would happen to Memory? Therefore, *Cuphophron*, there is a Substance of the Soul that is as distinct from its Operations or successive Thoughts as physical Matter is from the different shapes and motions that take place within it.

# DIVINE DIALOGUES.

**Cuphiphron:** I am not yet convinced of that.

**Hylobares:** And now for your second argument, which would infer from our being certain that we think (even while we doubt whether there is any extended physical thing in the world, or perhaps while not thinking of extension at all) that our minds therefore have no relation or connection to any extension whatsoever. You may easily discover the weakness of this reasoning if you only consider this: the intensity <note>original: "Intension"; here meaning the degree or strength of a quality</note> of heat or motion is considered without any relation to extension, and yet it is related to an extended object—for example, a glowing hot iron. Similarly, we can think without thinking at all of time or the movement of the sun; yet our thought is still subject to time. By observing the sun's motion, we can say precisely that a thought did not begin until a certain minute of an hour, and that it ceased by another specific minute. 

The same logic applies to place as it does to time; that is to say, a person's thoughts can be definitively said to have been conceived in a specific place, just as they are conceived within a specific time. To conclude, it seems like a mere fallacy <note>original: "Sophism"</note> to argue that because we can separate things in our thoughts, the things themselves are actually separated from each other in reality. It is even worse to infer that they have no relation or connection to one another at all. 

If they were indeed so unrelated in a full and complete understanding of them—both in their circumstances and their essence—then I admit your conclusion might be valid. But when the mind is stretched on a metaphysical rack to pull apart things that are found together in nature, and then claims they have no relation to each other—or when it accidentally leaves out what cannot be excluded from the perfect *idea* of such a being—then all conclusions drawn from such principles must be like the principles themselves: defective or distorted. And therefore, being so dissatisfied with *Cuphiphron's* solution to the current difficulty...

<margin>36. That God is essentially present everywhere.</margin>
**Philotheus:** I will, *Hylobares*, and I believe you will find it one of the easiest you have proposed <note>original: "propounded"</note>, though I must confess it may seem strange at first glance. It has seemed so to very famous scholars <note>original: "Criticks"</note> in matters of theology who—mainly from the consideration that the foul and bad-smelling places of the Earth are an unfit container <note>original: "Receptacle"</note> for the Divine Presence—have dared to limit the Divine Nature <note>original: "Godhead"</note> to the heavens. This opinion of theirs is to be attributed more to the sensitivity of their senses than the sharpness of their intellect <note>original: "sagacity of their Wit"</note>. For all those things that seem so foul and disagreeable in nature are not *really* so in themselves, but only *relatively*. What is one creature’s *poison* is the *delight* and food of another, and what is the *death* of one is the *life* of the other. So we may easily imagine that, although God has an awareness of whatever exists, there is no necessity at all that he should be negatively affected, disgusted, or in any way bothered by being present with anything. On the contrary, it is impossible that he should be, since everything that implies imperfection is incompatible with the Divine **Essence**...

Furthermore, there are many *incompossibilities* <note>original: "Incompossibilities"; things that cannot exist or happen at the same time</note> and *instabilities of matter* <note>original: "Lubricities of Matter"</note> that cannot have the same conveniences and fitness in every shape or form. Indeed, matter would not be fit for anything if its shapes and forms were not varied in an almost infinite way.

**Hylobates:** I partly understand you, **Philotheus**; please, go on.

**Philotheus:** Therefore, I infer that the measure of God's *Providence* is still his Goodness. This is because those *incompossibilities* in matter are unavoidable; and whatever designed or permitted evil there seems to be in Providence, it exists for a far greater good. Therefore, it is not properly counted as evil when one calculates the total summary of the affairs of the Universe.

Furthermore, the tears of those who suffer are often the mother of compassion in the spectators and extort their help. Likewise, the news of but one ridiculous mistake fills the mouths of a thousand men with mirth and laughter; and the fact that everyone is universally liable to be laughed at makes every man more careful in his manners and more cautious in his affairs, especially where his path is most slippery.

To this he adds the infestation of wild beasts that are so terrible and hurtful to mankind both by land and sea, and the unhealthiness <note>original: "Morbidness"</note> of the seasons of the year.

### VIII. *Of Diseases.*

*Hylobares.* That is shrewdly suggested, *Philotheus*. But even if we admit the necessity of dying, what necessity or benefit is there in the frequency of *diseases*? This is a topic in *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher who argued that the flaws in nature proved the world was not created by a deity.</note> which *Sophron* forgot to address.

*Philotheus.* As for *diseases* in general, *Hylobares*, they are as necessary a consequence of our earthly nature as death itself. However, just as death would visit us more slowly, so would *diseases* strike less fiercely and frequently if it were not for our own intemperance and irregular passions. We are to blame for what we find most intolerable; we should not criticize Providence, which has contrived all things for the best and has allowed nothing to happen without mature judgment and deliberation. For *diseases* themselves, though they are the natural results of a mortal constitution, may well be approved of by Divine Wisdom for several reasons. First, while they are being endured, they improve the minds of those who are good and serve as a just punishment to those who are evil. Furthermore, the pleasure of recovery usually more than compensates for the past misery in both cases. Therefore, neither has much cause to complain about the neglect of Providence in such visitations.

*Bathynous.* Indeed, I think that mankind has so little reason to complain that they have, instead, a very high obligation to admire and praise that Providence which allows so many "outward evils," as they are called, to roam the world. For when they strike, they frequently put us in a position to seriously reflect on the duties of piety and virtue—reflections we would never encounter, despite all our boasts of free will, unless these heavy weights were cast into the balance to counter our inclinations <note>original: "propensions"</note> toward following the lusts and pleasures of life and the ordinary allurements of the world.

*Philotheus.* That is excellently well observed indeed, *Bathynous*.

*Philoth.* As an example: when someone shoots at a flock of pigeons or a group of ducks, do you expect that Divine Providence should so guide the shot that it hits none except those it kills outright, and never sends any away with a broken leg? And, what is of greater importance, the judge should be struck dumb as soon as he begins to give a sentence against the innocent; the sword should fall out of the hand of him who maintains an unjust quarrel; the lips of the priest should be miraculously sealed up as soon as he begins to vent false doctrines and delude the people with lies; and the dangerous medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> of either an unskillful or villainous physician should never be able to find its way to the mouth of the gullible patient. 

The meaning of this would be that God should make man a free creature, and yet violently force him to act only one way. This would make the various faculties of the soul useless, prevent the variety of social orders among men, silence these busy actors on the stage of the Earth, and by this obvious interference, as it were, bring *Christ* to judgment before the proper time. Thus, the ignorance and impatience of the unskillful would end the theater production before the play is half finished, because the complexity of the plot makes the spectacle tedious to those who do not understand it. 

But let the atheist know there will be a "God from the machine" <note>original: "Deus ex machina"; a theatrical term for a god who appears at the end of a play to resolve all problems</note>—*Christ* coming in the clouds—who shall resolve everything, and whom the atheist shall see at length to his own sorrow and confusion. *Philop.*

<summary>Philotheus argues that if God constantly intervened to prevent every accident or moral evil, human free will would be meaningless and the "drama" of earthly life would be cut short. ### DIVINE DIALOGUES

Therefore, the *Cartesian Hypothesis* <note>The theory of René Descartes that animals are mere machines or "automata" without souls or feelings.</note> in this case is so far from helping to resolve any difficulty in Divine Providence, that it would be the greatest demonstration in the world against God's goodness if it were true. Namely, that such an infinite number of animals, as we call them—creatures capable of truly existing and enjoying a vital happiness—should be made as mere senseless puppets, devoid of all the joys and pleasures of life.

*Hylas:* I expect a better answer from *Philotheus*, or else I shall be left very much in the dark.

*Philotheus:* My answer, in brief, is this: this is the sport that Divine Wisdom affords the contemplative mind in the study of her works. She puzzles them at first sight, even to the point of making herself suspected of some oversight, or of having committed some offense against the sacred nature of God—which is *Goodness* and *Justice* itself. Yet, after scanning the matter more accurately, they find it most agreeable to that rule. This is certainly the case here. For what is so just as that aphorism of *Pythagoras's* school: "The lesser exists for the sake of the greater" <note>original: *Tò χείρον ἕνεκα τῶ βελτίονος*</note>? And what is such good wisdom as to contrive things for the highest enjoyment of all? 

For I say, as I said before, that Divine Providence, in the generations of fishes, birds, and beasts, included in her calculations the "supernumeraries" <note>term: extra individuals produced in excess of what the environment can support</note> that were to be food for the rest. And *Hylobares* must prove whether so many individuals of these species could come into the world and continue in succession if their numbers were not reduced by this seemingly cruel law of feeding upon one another. Furthermore, we see various species of living creatures provided for in the most pleasant and transporting way by this method. For how delightful a thing it is for them, by their craft and agility of body, to become masters of their prey! Even men, who make for themselves a fortune...

Let them be the judges whether they would rather have their fortunes determined by their own intelligence, strategy, and courage. When something of importance is being hunted, it makes the pleasure of the game more substantial; it fills the mind and body with more vigor and eagerness, and makes the victory more satisfying and valuable. Just as running for a bet makes a man use his limbs with more courage and speed, and makes him feel more pleased that he has overcome his opponent. Therefore, the animal life in beasts and birds (and they were never intended for anything higher) is highly gratified by this exercise of their strength and cunning; yet, the species of all things are still very abundantly preserved. 

To complain that certain numbers of animals must be "lopped off"—creatures who must die eventually anyway—is misguided. If they lived and reproduced without any such restraint, they would become a burden to the Earth and to themselves for lack of food. Such a complaint is merely the objection of our own *softness* and ignorant *sentimentality* <note>original: "effeminacy," used here in the archaic sense of being over-sensitive or weak-minded</note>, not a just charge against God or Nature. For Divine Wisdom, having freely and generously provided for the whole of creation, does not dote on this or that specific individual as humans do, but willingly lets them go for a more substantial and more universal good. 

As for *cattle* <note>original: "beeves"</note> and sheep, the more common food of man, how often is the farmer at a loss for grass and fodder for them? # DIVINE DIALOGUES

We imagine <note>original: "phanfy"</note> brutes as if they were men, when in reality they have no other law than the common law of nature, which is the law of *self-love*. They will satisfy the cravings of that self-love, regardless of what is inconvenienced by it. Just as fire will burn if it takes hold—even to the consumption of a whole forest—despite the fact that the wood never did the fire any harm to deserve such treatment; so every animal would satisfy its own craving appetite, even if it meant devouring all the rest of the world. Every sparrow, titmouse, or swallow would do this. So, if you indulge that imagination, they are all equally wicked; and therefore it should not seem so harsh that the devourers are also to be devoured. But the most true and philosophical understanding is to attribute no more wickedness to devouring brutes than to swallowing gulfs of the sea or devouring fire.

**XII.** <margin>Of the *rage* of the elements, the poison of serpents, and the wrath of wild beasts.</margin> **Hylobares:** Why, *Philotheus*, that is the very thing I was going to object to next; I mean, the rage of the elements as well as the wrath of wild beasts, and the various monstrosities of creatures that occur, whether as entire species or single individuals. And as for the wrath of beasts, there is nothing more diabolical in it than natural anger <note>original: "choler"</note> and the flames of fire, which do no more hurt than the pure beams of the sun passing through a pure glass, whose shape alone makes them burn. But if these kinds of creatures carry any mischief or poison in their teeth, tails, or their whole body, that poison is nothing but a mismatch <note>original: "disproportionality"</note> of their particles to the particles of our own or other animal bodies. But we must not make our own hatred the measure and true estimate of the nature of others. For those poisonous creatures are not poisonous to their own kind; they are so far from mutual hatred that they are joined in the nearest link of love possible, by which they propagate their *species*. 

Therefore, these objects of such a terrible appearance are not evil in themselves. They are capable of the delights of the *animal* life as well as any other creature. Furthermore, because they are so remarkably dreadful to behold, they serve as living symbols of that attribute of *Power* when it is not tempered with *Goodness*. They were rightly brought into being in this region of sin as ready instruments of divine wrath, notable ornaments of the theater of the world, and a great enrichment of the history of nature. Nature would be defective if it did not run from one extreme to another; for even a variety of sweet things becomes sickening <note>original: "cloy"</note>, and there is no remedy so good as a mixture of sharp, bitter, and sour.

## XVI.
<margin>How the entrance of sin into the world can consist with the goodness of Providence.</margin>

*Cuph.* I am even glad at heart to see *Hylobares* so much puzzled with this difficulty, as it gives me the opportunity, with *Philotheus’s* leave, to raise him into as high a pleasure by the agreeableness and clarity <note>original: "perspicuity"</note> of the solution. *Philoth.* I pray you proceed then, *Cuphophron*; I hope your success will be the better for it.

*Cuph.* That I shall do right willingly. We shall not have so venomous a conception concerning the creation of God, or be cast into the errors of *Manicheism* <note>A dualistic religious movement that taught the world was created by an evil power rather than a good God.</note> or *Gnosticism*, imagining we see the sign of the Devil's paw, or smelling the sulfur of Hell in everything as strongly as one smells the "Bishop's foot" <note>A common 17th-century proverb for milk that has been burnt to the bottom of a pot.</note> in milk burnt to the bottom of a skillet.

Even if there were no absolute necessity in nature for this to exist (as we sometimes see the affections of creatures directed so much toward others that they forget themselves), it was still appropriate for Divine Providence to establish this principle in them all: that every thing should love itself very heartily and provide for itself. Just as the roots of trees, without any moral hesitation, draw to themselves all the nourishment they are capable of—not caring which other tree withers so long as they flourish—there is, in this behavior, nothing of either the Devil or of sin.

But it is now manifest that Providence acted very well in implanting such a sharp *self-love* in every animal. For those more notable *functions* of *animal life*, such as those depending on strength and agility, craft and sagacity <note>Wisdom or keen perception.</note>, could not be exercised to any significant degree without this principle. A crow would not have the heart to peck at a worm, nor a swallow to snatch at a fly. The same reasoning applies to those more notable and industrious ambushes <note>original: "Insidiations"</note> of other stronger and more crafty creatures that hunt for their prey. Besides, every animal, in respect to itself, has in some sense or measure a resemblance of that divine attribute of *omnipresence*; for wherever it may be, it cannot leave itself behind. Why not keep his creature within the bounds of his own laws by communicating to all men and angels such an irresistible measure of grace that they could never have possibly been disobedient to him?

*Philoth.* To this, *Hylobares*, I answer: God having made a free creature—and it is impossible to prove that he did wrong in making it—Omnipotence itself (if I may speak with reverence) is not able to set aside certain unavoidable relationships or congruities <note>original: "congruities"; logical fitness or points of agreement</note> that this creature bears to the Divine Attributes. For example, it is a thing utterly unimaginable that even the eternal Intellect of God should be able to produce a finite number that did not bear a certain proportion to some other finite number first given. This free creature, therefore, having been made, necessarily faces the several attributes of God with various relationships. And this native freedom in the creature challenges His Wisdom to show her best skill in dealing with a creature that is free, doing as little violence to its nature as possible. We see that the Wisdom of God has practiced this same principle upon Matter, as I noted a while ago. And yet, the defacement of rightly-organized Matter is as real an encroachment upon, or opposition to, what is intellectual or divine—I mean the Divine *Ideas* <note>original: "Idea's"; referring to the Platonic concept of perfect forms in the mind of God</note> themselves—as...

<summary>Philotheus argues that God's goodness remains the measure of providence even in punishment, explaining that God respects the free will of His creatures rather than using irresistible grace to force obedience.</summary>

Just as Divine Wisdom, therefore, does not force terrestrial matter beyond the bounds of its own natural capacity—such as protecting all animal bodies from diseases and death—no more should the universal Divine Goodness *irresistibly* prevent all free creatures from using their own nature. Therefore, being free, they ought to be put to the trial to see what they will do, according to the fitness of their condition. 

If a failure occurs due to very strong temptations that almost overpowered the strength of the free creature, this state of the case is a fitting object of the *mercy* of God. But if the creature has strength enough, and has been often and earnestly invited to stay close to and pursue those things that are best, and yet perpetually slights them and shuffles them off, the party offending in this way is a fitting object of divine *slight* and *scorn*. It is only just that such a person be left to follow his own "swinge" <note>original: "swindge"; meaning his own natural inclination or unchecked impulse</note> and to find the fate that attends such wild courses. For it seems a kind of disparagement to pin virtue and divine grace upon the sleeves of those who are unwilling to receive it. It would be as unseemly as forcing a rich, beautiful, and virtuous bride upon some poor, slouching clown <note>original: "Clown"; here meaning a rustic, unrefined, or foolish person</note> whether he wanted her or not.

Yet, rather than let everyone go to ruin, I see no inconsistency in God, as it were, laying violent hands upon some to pull them out of the fire, making them potent—though not irresistible—instruments for pulling others out as well. It is also morally impossible for others who have arrived at a certain level of the Divine Life <note>The "Divine Life" refers to a state of spiritual maturity and union with God's will.</note> to fall away. It is like the motion of bodies: whatever energy one loses is transferred to another; or like the beams of the sun, which, being reflected from one body, are received by another, and nothing is lost. What is rejected by some is, by the wisdom of God, so unavoidably conveyed upon others. But that it is best that all should partake alike of the overflowings of God will, I think, be no less difficult to prove than that all subordination of estates <note>social ranks or hierarchies</note> and conditions in the world should be taken away; or that God should not have created any of the more lowly and contemptible kinds of creatures, such as the worm, the fly, the frog, and the mouse. 

Therefore, it being so disputable a point whether it is not in itself as good that there should be those who are rightly called evil and wicked in the world, as that there should be such lowly or more mischievous creatures on the face of the earth, it is an inexcusable piece of rashness to conclude that the permission of sin is any valid argument against the goodness of that Providence that guides all things. For why should God <note>The original text implies the Divine Power or Providence</note> generally force or certainly determine the faculties of men that are naturally free, and so perpetually keep them from committing sin, when sin itself is so pompously led captive by the power of righteousness?

And as for that civil person whose child I strangled in the cradle, it was done in great mercy to him, and was no real hurt to the child, who is now with God. If that child had lived—whereas this gentleman had previously been piously, charitably, and devoutly inclined—I saw that his mind would have unavoidably sunk into the love of the world out of love for his child. Because he had no children before and doted so immensely on this one, I took away this momentary life from the body of the child so that the soul of the father might live forever.

->*The Prosperity of the Wicked, and the Affliction and Adversity of the Good.*<-

<margin>XXV. That the adversity of the good, and the prosperity and impunity of the wicked in this life, are no arguments against the accuracy of Providence.</margin>

For first, what is alleged concerning the impunity <note>original: "Impunity"; exemption from punishment</note> of the wicked is not only false, but impossible. For how can the wicked escape punishment, when wickedness itself is one of the greatest penalties? Or how can they be said to be prosperous, who have nothing succeed according to their own true aim and meaning? For every man means well, as Socrates wisely determines; but it is the perpetual unhappiness of the wicked that he does that which is evil. So great is his ignorance and lack of self-control <note>original: "Impotency"</note>, that he cannot reach the mark he aims at; but wishing the best for himself, as all other men do, yet notwithstanding he really pursues that which is worst. And therefore, in the eyes of the wise, he can be no object of envy, but only of pity. It is an unsuitable thing that any judgment concerning Divine Providence should be decided by the votes of fools. 

When a drunken man breaks glass windows, ravishes women, stabs men in the streets, and commits many such villainies as these, I appeal to you, Hylobares, what privilege or prosperity is there in this? Even if he were not to be punished by the magistrate, he has done that which indeed he had no true desire to do, but did heartily detest and abhor when he was sober. This is the true state of all wicked men whatsoever; let their power be ever so high, yet they act like drunkards or men in a dream, doing such things as they will be ashamed of as soon as they are sober or awakened.

Sophron. This is the very philosophy of the Apostle, O Philotheus: *What fruit had you then in those things whereof you are now ashamed?* <note>A reference to Romans 6:21.</note>

Philotheus. Now as it is evident, Hylobares, that they are punished in the loss <note>original: "forfeiture"</note> of that high happiness which consists in the peace and joy of a purified mind, wherein resides the true knowledge...

<summary>Philotheus argues that the wicked are never truly unpunished because wickedness itself is a penalty that prevents a person from achieving their true desire for good. He likens the actions of the wicked to those of a drunkard who commits acts he will later regret, suggesting they deserve pity rather than envy.</summary>

Just as there is a knowledge of God and a living sense of the beauty <note>original: "Comeliness and Pulchritude"</note> of grace and virtue, so likewise there is an infliction of internal pain to the very senses of the wicked. For what torture can be greater than that rack of pride, those scorpion-stings of envy, or those insatiable, scorching flames and torches of the Furies—untamed lust? What is worse than strangling care, or the severe sentences of their own anxious fears? What dungeon is more foul <note>original: "noisome"</note>, horrid, or dismal than their suspicious ignorance and the oppressing loads of sudden grief and melancholy?

Again, it is further manifest that the wicked are plagued even in this life; for they are a mutual plague and scourge to one another, taking turns acting as executioners and hangmen. Indeed, all the noise of injury and injustice in the world is ordinarily nothing else but a complaint that wicked men are abusing one another. Therefore, why should it be expected that Divine Providence should immediately take vengeance on the very executioners of His own justice?

But as for those few righteous people who are in the world, they are actually made better by those things that seem to the ignorant <note>original: "Idiot and unskilful"</note> to be the only evils that mortals can suffer. The unhappiness <note>original: "Infelicity"</note> of the godly commonly arises from this: they try to scramble with the men of this world for the very things that are the most fitting "happiness" for the wicked. Because the godly fight with them like roosters on their own dunghill, it is no wonder they get the worst of it; for as the Scripture says, *this is their hour and the power of darkness.* <note>A reference to Luke 22:53.</note>

Thirdly, it is manifest that the peace and lack of punishment <note>original: "Impunity"</note> of the wicked is very useful for exercising the virtues of the righteous. Through this, the righteous may discern their own sincerity or hypocrisy, and discover whether it is the pure love of piety that makes them act as they do, or merely the desire for the praise and approval of

Of men; whether the profession of their faith in God and of future happiness be formal <note>original: "formal" meaning outward or superficial</note> or real. For if it be real, what will they not be able to undergo? And what a high cordial <note>original: "Cordial" meaning a stimulating medicine or comfort for the heart</note> must it be unto them to have an unfeigned sense and belief of that great compensation they are to receive in the world to come? Not to mention what a great satisfaction the consciousness of constant sincerity is to the soul of a man even in this life also. Therefore, the strokes of the confusion and unrighteous disorder in the world do, in a manner, miss the righteous and hit heavy only where they should: upon the ungodly themselves. 

But as for what reaches those who are deemed more just, they are in all reason and modesty to look upon it as either a punishment for some relics <note>original: "Reliques" meaning remaining traces</note> of vices in them, or as an exercise of their virtues, so that God may be glorified in them. Therefore, if anything harsh happens to a good man, he will immediately examine himself to see if his heart be clean. If it is not, he is to look upon the event as a chastisement; if it is clean, he will bear it and embrace it as a trial from God, and as an occasion by which he may glorify the power of God within him. But if he does not do this, it is a sign his heart is not clean, and therefore why should he grumble that he is punished?

Fourthly, that tyranny, murder, perjury, blasphemy, and exorbitant lust have been notoriously and exemplarily punished by a kind of divine vengeance—and beyond all the expectations of men, even in this life, in several persons—is so noted in history that I need name no instances. But to pursue every monstrosity of wickedness with immediate punishment here in this world would not be to make men good, but rather to hinder the wicked from harming <note>original: "mifchieving"</note> and scourging one another, and from exercising the virtues of the righteous. 

Fifthly, in that wickedness is not so constantly and adequately punished in this life, there is also...

There is also this convenience in it: that it is a strong <note>original: "shrewd"</note> argument to any impartial person who understands the nature and attributes of God, that there is a reward to come hereafter in the other life.

To all of which I add in the last place, that the affairs of this world are like a curious, but intricately contrived, comedy. We cannot judge the direction of what is past or what is acting at present before the entrance of the last act, which shall bring in Righteousness in triumph. Though she has endured many a blow and has been very cruelly and despitefully used until now in the world, yet at last, according to our desires, we shall see the knight overcome the giant. And then I appeal to you, Hylobares <note>A character name meaning "lover of matter," representing a materialist viewpoint in the dialogue.</note>, whether all things have not been carried out according to the natural taste of your faculties. 

For what is the reason we are so much pleased with reading romances and the fictions of poets, but that here—as Aristotle says—things are set down as they *should* be? In the true history of the world until now, things are recorded indeed as they *are*, but that is only a testimony that they have not been as they should be. Therefore, in the conclusion of it all, if we shall see that come to pass which so greatly pleases us in reading the most ingenious plays and heroic poems—that long-afflicted Virtue at last comes to the crown—the mouths of all unbelievers must be forever stopped. 

For my own part, I do not doubt but that it will happen this way in the final closing of the world. But to impatiently call for vengeance upon every wickedness <note>original: "enormity"</note> before that time is rudely to overturn the stage before the entrance into the fifth act. It is to act out of ignorance of the plot of the comedy, and to prevent the solemnity of the general judgment by demanding more petty and particular executions. These are briefly the six heads, Hylobares, which I might have insisted upon...
