### XXVII.
<margin>The marvelous observation in Hylobares of an outward lightheartedness and inward seriousness at the same time.</margin>

Philop. "It seems to me, *Hylobares*, that those tunes and that instrument are too light for the serious discourse we have had together for so many hours."

Hyl. "But I assure you, *Philopolis*, my thoughts were never more serious than while I was piping these easy airs on my flageolet <note>original: "Flagellet"; a small flute-like woodwind instrument</note>. For they are so familiar to me that I had no need to focus on them, and my mind indeed was wholly taken up with objects suitable to our recent theme. And even then, while I was playing these light tunes, I was recovering in my memory as well as I could some part of a philosophical song that I once knew by heart—words, tune, and all—which has no small connection to the matters of today's discourse."

Philop. "It is remarkable, *Hylobares*, that you should be able to attend to such contrary things—so light and so serious—at one and the same time."

Hyl. "That is no more, *Philopolis*, than what *Eusistor* did during his story of the Angel and the Hermit <note>original: "Eremite"; a religious recluse or hermit</note>. And yet I believe he did that at least twenty times with his forefinger and his thumb while rehearsing that excellent parable; though I saw his mind was so taken up with the weightiness of the meaning that his expression seemed as devout as that of the hermit who was the chief subject of the story."

Eusist. "I pray you, *Hylobares*, take this glass of wine as a reward for teasing your friend so handsomely to excuse yourself. See if it is as good for refreshing the memory as *Sophron* claims it is. For then I hope we shall hear you sing as attentively as you have been whistling distractedly all this time."

Hyl.

### THE THIRD DIALOGUE.

Philotheus, Bathynous, Sophron, Philopolis, Eusistor, Hylobares, Cuphophron.

<margin>I. Conjectures regarding the causes of that mirth which the meeting of certain persons naturally excites in one another.</margin>

Sophron. What tall instrument is this, Cuphophron, that you have brought so unexpectedly into your garden bower?

Cuphophron. Its height reveals what it is: a theorbo <note>A theorbo is a large, long-necked lute used in the 17th century for accompaniment.</note>. Having observed last night how musically inclined this company was, I have provided this more grave and refined instrument for those who wish to play and sing. I did this instead of bringing Hylobares’s whistle—which is more commonly played for bears or dancing dogs than for philosophers or persons of quality. Thus, according to the custom of Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher Pythagoras believed music could harmonize and heal the soul.</note>, we may dismiss our composed minds to rest with a solemn piece of music after our philosophical debates.

Sophron. You abound in all kinds of civility, Cuphophron. But do you not play this instrument yourself?

Cuphophron. No, alas! It is too tall for me; my fingers will not reach the frets. But sometimes, with a careless stroke, I strum the guitar and please myself with that easier melody.

Hylobares. And it would please anyone alive to see Cuphophron at that graceful exercise, just as I have sometimes caught him. He looks exactly like the sign at the other end of the street.

Cuphophron. This joker Hylobares, I dare say, means the sign of the "Ape and the Fiddle." This is his revenge for the disparagement I showed toward his beloved Syrinx, the Arcadian nymph <note>In Greek mythology, Syrinx was a nymph who turned into reeds to escape Pan; Pan then made the first "pan-pipes" (a whistle) from those reeds.</note>.

**Cuphron:** That is a very odd thing regarding the men of Arcladam, **Euistus**; I pray, what is it?

**Euistus:** When the woman is delivered of a child, she gets out of the bed as soon as she can and follows the business of the house. But the man lies in bed for a set number of days and performs all the duties of a mother to the infant, except for giving it suck. The neighbors come "a-gossiping" <note>visiting for social celebration</note> to the man thus lying in bed, just as in other countries they do to the woman. And those of Arcladam give this reason for the custom: because the mother had a sufficient share of trouble in carrying the child and bringing him forth, it is therefore fitting that the man should ease her now and take part of the care upon himself, as **Marco Polo** <note>original: Paulus Venetus</note> reports. <margin>Of the Eastern Regions, Book 2, Chapter 41.</margin>

**Cuphron:** If the men of that country had milk in their breasts—which several men have had, according to the testimony of many credible writers, philosophers, physicians, and anatomists—the custom would have been more plausible. But as it is, it has its reason, as you see; it was not a pure piece of <term>sottishness</term> <note>foolishness or stupidity</note> that led them to it.

But where the women rule the men, it is a sign they have more strength or wit, and therefore have a right to rule them. And indeed, where do they not rule them? ### IX.
<margin>Of the Pagans' cruelty to their enemies, and inhumane humanity to their friends.</margin> But, as I remember, there are some direful stories of the Pagans' cruelty to their enemies, and inhumane humanity to their friends, that, methinks, should a little turn his stomach, Euistor.

**Euist.** There are very savage customs recorded in Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> touching the Essedones, Axiacae, and Geloni. The last clothe themselves and their horses with the skins of their slain enemies; with that part of the skin that covers the head they make a cap for themselves, and with the rest they clothe their horses. The Essedones celebrate the funerals of their parents with great feasting and joy, eating their flesh minced and mingled with mutton (which is their manner of burying them); but tipping their skulls with gold, they make drinking cups of them. Similarly, the Axiacae drink from the heads of their slain enemies, as well as drink their blood in the field. In *Castilla del Oro* <note>A 16th-century Spanish province in Central America.</note> the inhabitants also eat their own dead. 

But in the island of Java, as Ludovico di Varthema <note>original: *Ludovicus Patritius*, an Italian traveler.</note> reports, the children do not, like the Essedones, eat their parents; instead, when they are old and useless, they sell them to the cannibals <note>original: *Anthropophagi*</note>. The parents do the same to the children if they are desperately and irrecoverably sick in the judgment of the physician. For they hold it the noblest kind of burial to be interred in the belly of a man, and not to be eaten by worms. If anyone exposes the body of his dead friend to worms, they hold it a crime that cannot be atoned for by any sacrifice. The laws also of the Sardoans and Berbiccae...

The customs of the *Sardinians* and the *Berbiccae* <note>original: "Berbicæ"</note>, which *Aelian* relates, are very savage; the one commanding sons to knock their fathers on the head when they have reached their dotage <note>The period of life in which a person is old and weak</note>, and the other prohibiting anyone from living above seventy years.

*Hylobares:* Stop there, *Euphilous*: let's hear what excuse the advocate of the Pagans <note>original: "Panyms"</note> can devise for these horrid customs.

*Cuphophron:* Truly, *Hylobares*, these things must seem very harsh to any civilized person, especially at first sight. But yet there seems, if we search further, to be something commendable at the bottom of some of these. For the parricide <note>The killing of a parent or near relative</note> committed by the *Sardinians* and *Berbiccae* seems to arise out of compassion for their parents; they cannot endure to see so sad a spectacle as helpless and wearisome old age—a heavy disease, and yet incurable by anything else but death. 

And those of *Java*, who sell either the parents their sick children, or the children their aged parents, to the cannibals, do it both to ease them of their pain and to procure for them, as they think, the most honorable burial. It is no small support for these barbarous customs that Sir *Thomas More's Utopia* allows painful and remediless diseases to be shortened by some easy way of death. This seems to me another kind of midwifery, to facilitate the birth of the soul into the other world, just as midwives do the entrance of the body into this one. This may be the reason why the *Essedones* are so joyful at the funerals of their friends, as they look upon it as their birthday into the next state of existence.

*Euphilous:* The *Thracians* do so indeed, if we believe *Pomponius Mela*, who adds that their wives contend over who should be buried with their dead husbands. The *Indians* do the same. 

<margin>Their killing men at funerals to accompany the dead.</margin>
And *Acosta* reports that the Kings of *Peru* and the nobles of *Mexico* had their wives, nearest friends, and servants killed at their funerals to bear them company into the other world.

But the most horrible description of a temple is that of the King of *Calicut’s* <note>original: "Calecut's"; a major trading city in India, now known as Kozhikode.</note>, where they worship his god *Deumo*. For he does not serve the true god *Tamerani* because, although he made the world, he has given up the government of it (as they imagine <note>original: "conceit"</note>) to *Deumo*. This temple has its entrance adorned with many devils made of wood, skillfully <note>original: "artificially"</note> turned and carved. <header>D I V I N E  D I A L O G U E S.</header>

**Euistor.** To say the truth, **Cuphophron**, I do not find myself so subtle and clear a philosopher as to tell you exactly what it is; but I think it is, first, that mankind should worship so ugly and detestable an object as the Devil; and then in the second place, that they should sacrifice so worthy and noble a thing as a **human body**, which is capable of becoming the **Temple of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note>, to such a hateful idol.

**Cuphophron.** I think you have answered very correctly and perceptively, **Euistor**, if you rightly understand what makes the Devil so detestable.

**Euistor.** Surely his **pride**, **cruelty**, and malice of **nature**, and the fact that all **love** and **goodness** are extinct in him; if he could recover those, he would immediately become an **Angel of Light**.

**Bathynous.** **Euistor** has answered excellently well, and like a **mystical theologian**.

**Euistor.** To tell you the truth, I learned that from them.

**Cuphophron.** But if he has answered correctly, **Bathynous**, it is a sad consideration that we have in the civilized parts of the world those who profess a more hateful religion than the **Mexicans** <note>The author refers to the Aztec practice of human sacrifice, which was a common historical trope in the 17th century.</note> who sacrifice men to the Devil. I mean the **Superlapsarians** <note>original: "Superlapsarians"; a term for Calvinist theologians who believed God decreed the salvation or damnation of individuals before the Fall of Man occurred.</note>. # DIVINE DIALOGUES.

The Golden Key Paper puts all our controversies to an end; it declares *the measure of Providence to be the Divine Goodness, which has no bounds but itself, and which is infinite.* Therefore, it was the most disastrous accident that could ever have befallen the Philosophical Republic <note>original: "Philosophical Republick"—the community of philosophers and scholars</note>, that those two unlucky asses so rudely broke off *Bathynous's* conversation with that venerable sage. I surmise that in his intended discourse, he would have communicated the reasons and grounds for these conclusions to *Bathynous*. For true reason is so palpable and natural to a man that when he finds it, he feels himself fully satisfied and at ease.

*Philoth.* I commend your caution, *Hylobares*, in that you are so loath to build great conclusions upon weak or uncertain principles. Therefore, let me offer for your consideration a point of which I presume you will acknowledge yourself more certain: that is, *the possibility of the pre-existence of the soul*. I ask you, are you not very certain of that?

*Hyl.* Yes, surely I am; I see no contradiction <note>original: "repugnancy"</note> at all in it.

*Philoth.* Then you are not certain but that the soul does pre-exist.

*Hyl.* I confess it.

*Philoth.* And you are uncertain that it does not.

*Hyl.* That cannot be denied; it is the same thing, I think, that I granted before.

*Philoth.* Therefore, *Hylobares*, you make yourself liable to rebuke <note>original: "obnoxious"—in this context meaning vulnerable to criticism or at fault</note> both by *Providence* and by myself. You are at fault toward *Providence* because you bring forward uncertain allegations and accusations against her, and so spoil the beauty and perfection of her ways—which are so justifiable where they are perfectly known—by opposing her with fancies and notions that you yourself acknowledge you are not certain of. You are at fault toward *me* because you agreed with me at the beginning never to allege uncertain *hypotheses* <term>theories or proposed explanations used as a starting point for reasoning</term> against known truth.

*Philoth.* No science <note>original: "Art"</note> nor divine revelation <note>original: "Oracle"</note> that I know of has declared it so. How vastly distant then are those little fixed stars that show only as scattered shimmering dust <note>original: "Pin-dust"; referring to the tiny metallic filings produced when making pins</note> on a frosty night? At what immense distances are they from one another?

They are the words of the Prophet *Baruch*.

*Hyl.* It seems then that the *infiniteness* of the world is declared by that revelation rather than its *finiteness*.

# DIVINE DIALOGUES.

*Cuphophron.* I shall, Philotheus.

*Philotheus.* Was there not a first six thousand years of duration from the beginning of the world, assuming it began as long ago as you have described?

*Cuphophron.* According to my *hypothesis*, it began from eternity, and therefore the numbering of years from this time back to that will have no end <note>original: *exitus*</note>. We shall never reach the first six thousand years.

*Philotheus.* That is true, Cuphophron; but you answer cleverly, and yet you clearly imply that there was a first six thousand years, even if we cannot reach them. That is only because we begin at the wrong end of the timeline. By the same fallacy, you might conclude that there is not a "last" six thousand years if you began your count from eternity (as you call it), because your numbering would find no end <note>original: *exitus*</note> for us. And yet, suppose we are at this moment in the final second of the last six thousand years; we shall always be in the midst of some "last" six thousand years, or at least have lived through such divisions of time.

*Cuphophron.* That cannot be denied.

*Philotheus.* Therefore, Cuphophron, focus your attention <term>original: "animadversion"; here meaning the act of turning one's mind toward a subject</term> on the right end—that is to say, on the beginning of this infinite duration, as you imagine it. ## THE FOURTH DIALOGUE.

### Philotheus, Bathynous, Sophron, Philopolis, Euistor, Hylobares, Cuphophron.

<margin>I. A brief summary of what has happened so far in their discussion.</margin>
*Philoth.* Our conversation so far, *Philopolis*, has been spent either in briefly proving the *existence of God*, in clarifying His *attributes*, or in defending His *providence*. This was a necessary preparation for those who doubt these things, to ensure the proper understanding of the *mysteries of His kingdom*. For if there is no *God* nor any *Divine providence*, there can be no *Kingdom of God* on *Earth*, as *Hylobares* rightly noted at the start. And indeed, if the *providence of God* is not everywhere, it is a very suspicious matter <note>original: "suspicable business"</note> that it exists anywhere at all. This shows the necessity of accepting such *hypotheses* <note>original: "Hypotheses"; here referring to logical frameworks or assumptions</note> that will make sense of all occurrences and appearances of things we encounter in any nation on *Earth* or part of the *universe*. I believe such principles were those suggested in our last two days of conferences. If *Hylobares* (who seemed to be the only man unsure about these points) is now fully satisfied, I am ready to serve you, *Philopolis*, to the best of my ability regarding your questions about the *Kingdom of God*.

*Philop.* I humbly thank you, *Philotheus*. My strong desire to hear you speak on such an important *theme*, and my fear <note>original: "jealousie"; here meaning an anxious concern</note> that we will be very short on time <note>original: "streightned in time"</note>, makes me beg you to begin the matter without any further delay.

**Bathynous.** Why, **Cuphophron**, what greater problem is there in that than in the *Kingdom of Nature* and the *Kingdom of God* being the same thing <note>original: "coincident"</note>, which you do not seem to deny?

**Cuphophron.** I think it sounds very odd. Besides, we can imagine a ranking <note>original: "subordination"</note> between the *Kingdom of God* and the *Kingdom of Nature*. But the *Kingdom of God* and the *Kingdom of the Devil* seem to be in total opposition to each other, and therefore they cannot possibly be parts of the same kingdom.

**Bathynous.** That is a clever point, **Cuphophron**, regarding the outward sound of the words. But look into the internal <note>original: "intrinsecal"</note> nature of things. Place the beasts of the field and the devils of hell side by side, and tell me: what difference makes the one incapable of being members of the Kingdom of God more than the other? Is it because the devils have more cunning <term>subtilty: cleverness or craftiness</term> than the animals of the field? That would insultingly imply that the Kingdom of God is a city of fools. Is it because one is spiritual and the other physical? That reasoning would also exclude the good angels, who are the finest part of God's Kingdom. Is it because the devils are fallen <term>lapsed: having fallen from a state of grace</term>? Yet their "fall" is only into the *animal life*, the deepest root and source of which is *self-love* or *selfishness*. This stands in opposition to that other source or root of the *divine life*, which is the *pure love of God*, or the love of that which is simply and absolutely good. But *self-love* or *selfishness* is just as much the root of life in brute animals as it is in devils. Therefore, it seems obvious that in reality, the devils are just as capable of being part of the Kingdom of God as the animals are.

**Cuphophron.** The difference, **Bathynous**, seems to be this: the animals keep the integrity of their nature, but the devils have degenerated from their original condition and abandoned the position God had placed them in.

These things are utterly incompatible with God, who is infinitely better than all of Creation and is only capable of doing them good, but is not capable of receiving any good from them.

O *Cuphophron*, explain to us that the word *tyrant* <note>original Greek: τύραννος</note> anciently signified nothing worse than that; that is to say, an absolute monarch, a person invested with absolute sovereignty or power.

*Hyl.* But I ask you, *Philotheus*, upon what is this vast and unlimited sovereignty of God founded? Is it in His omnipotence, or in what? For some say absolute and irresistible power can do no wrong.

*Philoth.* That is a thing, *Hylobares*, I could never yet understand: that the most omnipotent power imaginable can ever have a right to do what is wrong—that is to say, to create any evil that is truly so upon the full calculation of all circumstances, or in the entire comprehension of the whole management <note>original: Oeconomy</note> of the universe. No *power*, though ever so *omnipotent*, can claim a right to such an act, any more than any *intellect*, however *omniscient*, can claim a right to authentically think that what is really false is true.

But in answer to your main question, regarding where the right of this absolute sovereignty in God is founded, I must tell you both clearly and concisely at once: that to *infinite, permanent, and unchangeable goodness*, there belongs by right both *omniscience* and *omnipotence*—the one as her *secretary*, the other as her *retinue* <note>original Latin: *Satellitium*, meaning an escort or bodyguard</note>. But the infinitely good God is not only by *right*, but by *nature*, both *omniscient*—

**Hebrew Idiom:** For in the long run, it is to include all the kingdoms of the earth. But there is a more specific reason for calling it the *Kingdom of God*, based on a passage in the Book of *Daniel*:
<margin>Daniel 2:44</margin> *And in the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed.* Because of this, the *Kingdom of Christ* is called the *Kingdom of Heaven* and the *Kingdom of God*. For <margin>Daniel 9:25–26</margin> after *seven weeks and sixty-two weeks* (that is, sixty-nine weeks), the *Messiah was to be cut off.* At that point, the *Jewish* people ceased to be God's people under the *Mosaical Dispensation* <note>The religious system and laws established by Moses.</note>. Instead, <margin>Daniel 9:24</margin> *everlasting righteousness*—the *eternal law* or *religion of Christ*—was introduced. The *Jewish sacrifices* ceased because the *Son of God* was offered as a single *oblation* <note>A religious offering or sacrifice.</note> upon the *Cross* for the sins of the whole world. 

This marks the *beginning* <note>original: "Inchoation"</note> of the *Kingdom of God* so frequently mentioned in the *Gospel*. Although it was at first no larger than <margin>Matthew 13:31</margin> *a grain of mustard seed*, it soon spread far and wide across the *Roman* Empire and eventually became its master. Who but the <term>Creative Mind <note>original Greek: *ho demiourgos nous*</note></term>, or the Divine Word <note>original: *Logos*</note>? None can be said to fill out these robes but him. 

And it is apparent that *Aaron's* robes were not only a symbol of the universe but were designed according to its truest system. This is because the Ephod <note>a ceremonial vestment worn by the High Priest</note> and the breastplate, which were placed over the region of the heart <margin>Exodus 28:6</margin> (the heart being the "sun" of this "lesser world" of the human body), were woven of scarlet and purple, with gold and white silk. These colors plainly represent the intense heat and shining light of the sun—what the *Pythagoreans* called <term>the fire situated in the center <note>original Greek: *to pyr en mesō idrymenon*</note></term>—just as this Ephod and breastplate are placed in the center of *Aaron’s* body. 

The blue robe also resembles the part of the heavens that contains the planets, which the hanging pomegranates represent. The longer garment <note>original: "Stole"</note> decorated with "eye-work" represents the <term>Starry Heavens <note>original Latin: *Caelum Stellatum*</note></term>, where the stars look like many twinkling eyes; meanwhile, the bells represent the harmony of the universe.

*Hyl.* I understand you very well, for I have read a fuller description to the same effect in a recent author. Thinking about these correspondences <note>original: "Congruities"</note> of the *Israelite* symbols strikes my mind with marvelous pleasure. They are very admirable, *Bathynous*, and very delightful. Compared with their fulfillment in the *Christian* Church, they are solid evidence of God's perpetual and absolute <note>original: "peremptory"</note> Providence in managing the affairs of his own people and kingdom.

*Cuphophron.* And regarding the *invocation of the saints*, *Philopolis*, it seems to me free enough from all suspicion of idolatry. *Philopolis.* But to answer you, *Cuphophron*, from a legal perspective: I believe, as Tully <note>original: "Tully"; the Roman statesman and orator Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> mentions somewhere, that religion is that part of justice which concerns the Deity. One primary right belonging to God—the highest invisible power—is invocation. This right is based on His omniscience. For the sake of clarity, let us divide this omniscience into three areas: terrestrial, aerial, and heavenly. Together, these cover all places and the entire scope of divine omniscience. 

If God had, as if by a legal deed of gift, divided these shares and handed them over to the saints—which we see He has not—then they would have the foundation for the right of being invoked. However, because they lack this foundation, our invocation of them acknowledges a level of excellence in them that exists nowhere but in God. Thus, giving the right of worship to others that is due to God alone becomes an act of injustice against God, which is termed idolatry. This is made even worse by the impudent insult to God’s wisdom and goodness in assuming that what God chose to omit would have been more wise and good. What do you think of this, *Cuphophron*?

That mighty **earthquake** at the opening of the sixth seal denoted only the downfall of the **Pagan** religion. Indeed, the bloody vision of the winepress signifies no more than that, even though it refers to **Babylon** because of the number of furlongs, which are applicable to the **Papal States** <note>original: "Stato della Chiesa"</note>, as Mr. **Joseph Mede** <note>A famous 17th-century English scholar and expert on the Book of Revelation.</note> observes. The extinguishing of the Pope's power there, rather than the slaughter of his armies, is what is signified by it.

**Philopolis:** But that number is just as applicable to the Holy Land, as the same writer observes.

**Philotheus:** Be it so, **Philopolis**. In that case, the vision may have two faces: one regarding the **Roman** Church, the other regarding the **Jewish** people. The first provides a **political** meaning, as I have already suggested, and the other a more **mystical** meaning.

**Philopolis:** Such as what, I ask you, **Philotheus**?

<margin>Zechariah 12:10, 11.</margin>
**Philotheus:** It signifies the power of the passion of **Christ** upon the converted **Jews** to the killing off <note>original: "mortifying"</note> of all sin and wickedness in them. It signifies making their conversion and repentance do its perfect work until it utterly subdues the mystical **Edom** <note>In this context, "Edom" represents the old, sinful nature or the enemies of God's people.</note> within them, letting out his blood plentifully according to that prophecy in **Zechariah**: *And it shall come to pass in that day, etc.*

<meta>Philotheus and Euistor continue their discussion of the symbolic meaning of Ezekiel's vision of the wheels and cherubim, specifically debating whether they represent celestial orbs or the cycles of Divine Providence.</meta>

*Philotheus.* That is a notion as far removed from the ancient wisdom of the *Jews* as falsehood is from truth.

*Euistor.* Why, *Philotheus*, *Jonathan ben Uzziel* <note>A famous first-century translator of the Hebrew prophets into Aramaic</note> is expressly of this opinion, as you may see in <margin>Part 3, chapter 4.</margin> *Moses the Egyptian's* <note>Moses Maimonides</note> *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: *More Nevochim*</note>. And he provides strong reasons for it. For he shows how, in the repeated narration of the vision, a *wheel* is called a *globe* or *sphere*, which makes him always <margin>Ezekiel 10:13.</margin> translate *Ophannim* <note>Hebrew for "wheels"</note> as *Galgalim* <note>Hebrew for "spheres" or "whirling things"</note>. Therefore, to have a sphere within a sphere (as the text would then read), what could be more symbolic of the celestial orbs <note>The concentric shells believed in old astronomy to carry the planets and stars</note>? This is very notable. Besides, they are said to have *eyes* (which correspond to the stars) and their color to be like the appearance of chrysolite <note>original Greek: ὡς εἶδ. Θαρσείς, *hos eidos tharseis*</note> (as the *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> also translate it), which the *Latin* translates as *like the appearance of the sea* <note>original: *ut visio Maris*</note>, which is a sky-blue <note>original: *cæruleous*</note> color matching that of the heavens.

*Philotheus.* I confess, *Euistor*, that besides the authority of the Rabbi, this idea has a certain beauty to it; but it has no force or solidity at all. For although *galgal* <note>Hebrew: גלגל</note> signifies a globe and sphere, it signifies a *wheel* as well, and therefore it can be interpreted in the same sense that *ophan* <note>Hebrew: אופן</note> is—namely, as a *wheel*. Furthermore, *one wheel* is said to be *on the earth*; but no celestial orb is on the <margin>Ezekiel 1:15.</margin> earth. And *all* the wheels, for all I know, may be represented by that *one wheel*; and by the *earth*, *all the terrestrial regions of the universe* are meant. For *all four cherubim* or *living creatures* are <margin>Ezekiel 10:15.</margin> also said to be but *one*. What this means in the Kabbalistic <note>original: *Cabbalistical*, referring to Jewish mystical interpretation</note> style is easy enough to guess: there may be a wheel within a wheel in the same sense that *ben Uzziel* wanted a globe within a globe. There are smaller and larger cycles of Providence in human affairs, with one surrounding the other, and the completion of the smaller cycles happens before <note>original: *antecedaneous to*</note> the completion of the larger ones. This is a notable observation regarding the Church of God and in the fulfillment of types <note>Biblical events or persons that foreshadow future ones</note>.

<summary>Philotheus and Euistor debate whether the "wheels" in Ezekiel's vision represent the physical celestial spheres or the metaphorical cycles of Divine Providence in human history. Philotheus argues against the literal astronomical interpretation, favoring a mystical and providential one.</summary>

...and prophecies. Those with the farthest reach and widest scope are those wheels that are so awe-inspiring <note>original: "dreadful"</note> and amazing because of their vast size, as <margin>Ezekiel 1:18.</margin> the vision describes them. And such is that large, vast cycle of Providence which, beginning with the first "Let there be light" <note>original: *Fiat Lux*</note> in *Genesis*, does not end until the last thunderclap suggested in the *Book of Revelation*.

And since the color of the wheel is said to be "as the appearance of the sea" <note>original Latin: *tanquam visio Maris*</note>, that confirms our earlier explanation: those wheels are the turnings of Providence and the historical cycles of *kingdoms*, *peoples*, and *nations*, which the prophetic style compares to the *sea*.

Finally, the fact that they are said to be *full of eyes* indicates the assistance of the angelic orders in human affairs (their involvement and engagement with them). They are those many eyes of Providence watching over the earthly regions and directing all things according to their own purpose.
->But the gods accomplish all things according to their own mind. <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ δ' κτ' σφέτερον πάντα τελῶσι νόον</note><-

*Cuphophron.* These wheels of *Ezekiel* have made my mind think of the "wheel of fortune" all this time—that common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> expression so often on people's lips nowadays.

*Euistor.* Not only nowadays, *Cuphophron*, but it is as ancient as *Herodotus*. <margin>Clio, chapter 207.</margin> In his writings, this is the very language used by *Croesus* to King *Cyrus* in his speech concerning his battle with *Tomyris*, Queen of the *Massagetae*: "But if you realize that you are also a man, and that you rule over others like yourself, learn this first: that there is a wheel of human affairs, and as it turns, it does not allow the same people to be always fortunate." <note>original Greek: Εἰ δ' ἔγνωκας ὅτι ἄνθρωπος καὶ σὺ εἶς, καὶ ἑτέρων τοιῶνδε ἄρχεις, ἐκεῖνον πρῶτον μάθε, ὡς κύκλος τῶν ἀνθρωπήων ἐστὶ πραγμάτων, περιφερόμενος δὲ οὐκ ἐᾷ αἰεὶ τοὺς αὐτοὺς εὐτυχέειν</note>

*Cuphophron.* I see that this concept <note>original: "conceit"</note> of the wheel of fortune is much more ancient than I realized.

*Philotheus.* But because the concept is so early and so common, it shows how naturally it expresses the idea. This is a further confirmation of how simple and natural it is...
